How confident are we about its size?

The same stores, calculation, and decision—with the specification and reproducible steps visible.

Independent shelf audit · week 16 · 30 sampled stores

← Return to the worked analysis

Read here or present the same material, one step at a time.

Use the same analysis rows

The audit selects 30 stores without replacement and independently checks 140 product-days at each. The target is the equal-store mean expected stockout rate in week 16. These audit counts are distinct from the operating-system counts.

Case seed: 20261109. All ten labs use the same store IDs and underlying records. Read the shared data dictionary.

Reproduce the calculation

Compute the mean of the 30 audit rates, sample SD with denominator n−1, SE = SD/√n, and t(0.975,n−1). This introductory interval does not apply a finite-population correction; it is an approximate interval for the store-level audit mean.

audit = world()['audit']
a = audit.stockout_rate.to_numpy()
mean = a.mean()
sd = a.std(ddof=1)
se = sd / np.sqrt(len(a))
critical = t.ppf(.975, len(a)-1)
worked_interval = [mean-critical*se, mean+critical*se]
assert np.allclose(worked_interval, [lesson_result(3)['low'], lesson_result(3)['high']])

# Bootstrap sampled stores, then test the specified target.
audit = world()['audit'].stockout_rate.to_numpy()
rng = np.random.default_rng(SEED + 303)
boot = audit[rng.integers(0, len(audit), (2000, len(audit)))].mean(axis=1)
percentile_interval = np.quantile(boot, [.025, .975])
standard_error = audit.std(ddof=1) / np.sqrt(len(audit))
test_statistic = (audit.mean() - 10) / standard_error
one_sided_p = t.sf(test_statistic, len(audit)-1)
assert np.isclose(percentile_interval[0], lesson_result(3)['depth']['bootstrap_low'])
assert np.isclose(one_sided_p, lesson_result(3)['depth']['p_one_sided'])

# Paired observations retain their store identity.
audit_rows = world()['audit'][['store_id','stockout_rate']]
system_rows = world()['panel'].query('week==16')[['store_id','stockout_rate']]
paired = audit_rows.merge(system_rows, on='store_id', suffixes=('_audit','_system'), validate='one_to_one')
differences = paired.stockout_rate_audit - paired.stockout_rate_system
assert np.isclose(differences.mean(), lesson_result(3)['depth']['paired']['mean'])

The code runs after the shared setup in the notebook. The downloadable script includes that setup and runs on its own.

Read the model and uncertainty

The calculation takes stores as the independent sampling units. Between-store differences and within-store measurement variation both enter the observed spread of audit rates. A finite-population or multilevel analysis can refine the uncertainty when a sampling design requires it.

Change one analytical choice

Repeat the store sampling within the shared world and compare estimates with the known expected chain rate. Keep sample size fixed when studying sampling variation, then change sample size to study precision.

Connect the inference formulas

t = (estimate − null value) / estimated SE; CI = estimate ± t critical value × SE

For a one-sample mean, use n−1 degrees of freedom. For paired readings, apply that formula to the within-store differences. Welch’s test uses separate group variances and its approximate degrees of freedom. The mean audit interval is an approximate repeated-sampling procedure; the finite-population correction is not applied in this teaching calculation.

audit = world()['audit'].stockout_rate.to_numpy()
rng = np.random.default_rng(SEED + 303)
boot = audit[rng.integers(0, len(audit), (2000, len(audit)))].mean(axis=1)
np.quantile(boot, [.025, .975])

Unbiasedness concerns the estimator’s expectation across repetitions; consistency concerns convergence as information increases; efficiency compares sampling variance among estimators under stated conditions. These properties are distinct from whether the population itself is the one management wants to act on.

How this case is generated

The shared world contains 150 stores followed for 32 weeks. Delivery time, location, demand, promotions, store differences, and a common time pattern generate the probability of a stockout. Each store-week contains 140 product-days. The generator draws their availability and records both policy paths using the same underlying draws.

The expected alert reduction varies with delivery time and location. Offers are randomized only within the 50-store pilot cohort. Voluntary adoption uses measured starting conditions in a separate cohort. The final cohort starts a selected rollout in week 25. These are distinct studies inside the same business history.

Inspect the numerical mechanism

p0 = 0.055 + 0.014 × lead + 0.0005 × (demand − 100) + 0.018 × urban + 0.003 × (lead − 3) × urban + 0.020 × promotion + store effect + 0.006 × sin(week / 4)

Expected reduction = 0.006 + 0.008 × lead + 0.004 × urban; p1 = p0 − reduction

The probabilities are converted to counts by comparing 140 uniform draws with p0 or p1. Cost is 6 CU per stockout product-day plus 20 CU per week when alerts are offered. These costs are the stated management accounting scenario. The complete assignment rules, random streams, and calculations are in the shared source.

Read the shared generator and analysis source

Compare with the known answer

The shared world’s expected week-16 stockout rate across all stores is 11.43%. Compare that with the sample estimate and interval after making the decision.
